steps.title: Yes, you're right
steps.say: Good catch: in northern summer, Earth is actually a bit farther from the Sun, in early July. So distance can't be the cause.

ops.text: Yes! In July Earth is FARTHER from the Sun.
So distance is not what makes summer.

steps.title: Orbit is almost a circle
steps.say: Earth's orbit is nearly circular. The distance changes by only about 3 percent, which is too small to matter much.

ops.text:
Distance changes only about 3%
(147 million km vs 152 million km).

steps.title: Tilt changes sunlight
steps.say: What matters is the tilt. In July the northern half leans toward the Sun, so sunlight hits it more directly and days are longer.

ops.text:
Tilt toward the Sun: direct light + long days
= summer. Tilt away: slanted light = winter.

North leans toward
the Sun here?

steps.title: Label the seasons
steps.say: Opposite sides of the orbit give opposite seasons in the north and south. Summer in one hemisphere is winter in the other.

steps.title: Summary
steps.say: So seasons come from tilt, not distance. The tilt changes how directly sunlight strikes each hemisphere.
